title: What is known about 1RB0RC_1LC1RF_1RE0LD_1LC1LA_---1RD_0RB0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RC_1LC1RF_1RE0LD_1LC1LA_---1RD_0RB0RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The run is a Collatz-like process: a big block on the left is converted back and forth between two words, growing by a factor about 4/3 per cycle, while a small counter at the right end keeps the remainders. Shift rules are proved in Lean; the cycle map is observed, not decoded exactly, and no reduction of the halting question is given yet.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: Shift rules, for every length
claims.text: Going right: B crosses (10)^n unchanged, F crosses (01)^n unchanged, A turns each 011 into 110, B turns each 110 into 101; each for every n and every tape around.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 43,966 cells have been visited and 17,659 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.499). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.087).

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: tools/c/tmrun.c: 1010 steps from blank tape without a halt (57,846 ones).

claims.title: No closed tape language from windows up to 7
claims.text: bbtools.ctl with K = 2 to 7 closes but allows a halt (7 to 579 abstract halting configurations); n-gram CPS (widths 3 to 7, -H, -U) fails.

claims.title: The 4/3 cycle
claims.text: With the head in A at the left end the tape is a b (a = 10, b = 110), then one big block, then a short tail. The big block alternates between d^Y (d = 010) and a^X: from d^Y the sweeps usually build a^(2Y+2) (for example Y = 17,473 gives X = 34,948), and from a^X they build d-blocks of about 2X/3 plus what the tail contributes. The successive Y: 61, 83, 137, 195, 261, 357, 481, 667, 887, 1239, 1675, 2247, 3009, 4025, 5375, 7171, 9565, 12953, 17473, 23325 (to 2.9·109 steps), ratios about 4/3. The tail at the right end (runs such as d^24 a^14 d^8 a^8 d^8 a^8 d^4 a^2) changes only at the conversions: it holds the remainders.

claims.title: Where a halt would come from
claims.text: The halt is E reading a 0. E is entered only from C reading a 0 (going right); in 10<sup>9</sup> steps E was entered 5,798,513 times and always read a 1. A halt needs C, moving right, to meet two 0s in a row.

claims.title: Does it halt?
claims.text: Not known. The exact cycle map (how the remainder mod 3 of X and the tail combine) is not written down yet; with it the question should become a Collatz-like question about that map.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB1LF_1LC0RD_---1LD_1RB1RE_1LA0LB_0LA0LE up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 43,966 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: One big block and a small tail
html: With the head in A at the left end, and words a = 10, b = 110, d = 010, the tape at step 2,831,052,048 is
A>a b d a^34948 0 d^23 a d^10 a^26 d^8 a^8 d^8 a^8 d^4 a^2 1
A>a b d^23325 a d^2 a^32 d^16 a^26 d^4 b d^7 a^8 d^4 a^8 1
Almost all of the tape is one big block, written either with a or with d; the short tail on the right is a small counter.

sections.eyebrow: The rule from one cycle to the next
sections.heading: Double, then take two thirds
html: Sweep by sweep, the machine rewrites the big block from one word into the other. A block d^Y (three cells per unit) becomes a^(2Y+2) (two cells per unit): Y = 17,473 gave X = 34,948. A block a^X becomes a d-block of about 2X/3 units, the leftover (X mod 3) and a little from the tail being settled in the tail: X = 34,948 gave Y = 23,325. So Y grows by about 4/3 per cycle: 61, 83, 137, 195, 261, 357, 481, 667, 887, 1239, 1675, 2247, 3009, 4025, 5375, 7171, 9565, 12953, 17473, 23325. Each cycle sweeps a tape about 4/3 longer about 4/3 more often, which is why the left side looks like a bouncer while the tail, changed only once per cycle, grows like a logarithm.

sections.heading: Only E on a 0
html: The only halt is E reading a 0, right after C has read a 0 and moved right. In 109 steps this setup happened almost six million times and the second cell was always a 1. The places where something irregular happens are the conversions of the big block, where the remainder mod 3 is handed to the tail; whether a tail state can ever put two 0s in front of C is the open question.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.499). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.087).
After 109 steps the tape spans 43,966 cells (31,752 left of the start, 255 right), with a density of 1s of 0.402.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: One big block that alternates between (010)^Y and (10)^X: turning d's into a's doubles it, turning a's back into d's takes two thirds of it, so Y grows by about 4/3 per cycle (a Collatz-like 4/3 map), with the remainders kept in a small counter at the right end.
